title: Model-aware agent-loop tiers for the Claude 5-series lineup
description:
## Objective
Update /core:agent-loop's pipeline and model-selection guidance to be fully model-aware for the Claude 5-series lineup, WITHOUT duplicating stages that already exist in references/forge.md (Test Reviewer=opus and Final Reviewer=opus already exist there today; only the Plan row currently has no reviewer).

## Acceptance criteria
- (a) ONE genuinely new gate: add a Plan Reviewer role (fable) to Forge's Plan row in references/forge.md — the only row that currently lacks a reviewer
- (b) Everywhere else is a model-DEFAULT SWAP on existing roles, not a new stage: Test Reviewer opus->fable, Reviewer/Final Reviewer opus->fable
- (c) Document (no code change) that P2 Test Author=sonnet and P3 Implementer=sonnet already satisfy the sonnet-implementer/sonnet-test-writer ask. ALSO explicitly confirm/document — same treatment as the sonnet roles — that the Plan row's author remains opus (satisfies "opus planners") and that P1 Test Planner remains opus (satisfies "opus test planners"); do not leave these two implicit
- (d) Model Selection table gains explicit rows: text-based search/inventory -> haiku, test-commands/CI-commands -> haiku, Playwright/MCP-tool-driving agents -> sonnet
- (e) DROPPED: qa-playwright.md, qa-tidewave.md, and elixir/agents/tidewave.md already have model: sonnet set (verified by direct read) — no file change needed here, only the table row in (d) documents the existing convention
- (f) Every new/changed reviewer-role default gets its own AGENT_LOOP_*_MODEL env var, consistent with the existing no-hardcoded-model-literal rule (line ~99 of SKILL.md — verify this line number against A's post-conversion file, it will have shifted since A restructures this file): AGENT_LOOP_PLAN_REVIEWER_MODEL, AGENT_LOOP_TEST_REVIEWER_MODEL, AGENT_LOOP_REVIEWER_MODEL, AGENT_LOOP_FINAL_REVIEWER_MODEL — added to the existing env-var table (verify no name collision with the existing six vars). Default behavior is a capability fallback, not a single literal: attempt model: fable first; if the spawn errors because fable isn't available to the account/environment, retry the identical spawn with model: opus. Document this explicitly as the REVERSE of the existing haiku->sonnet->opus escalation ladder — that ladder promotes a task's model on repeated failure; this fallback degrades a reviewer's model on unavailability, and the two must not be conflated in the SKILL.md text. Same fallback applies to D1's comment-reviewer agent (claude-skills-291, which must have already landed — this issue is now blocked by it; cross-reference, don't redefine)
- (g) Final Reviewer gate: on a fixable finding, route to the Fix Agent per the EXISTING retry loop (do not delete it); escalate to the user only on an unresolvable finding or after the existing 2-promotion escalation cap is hit — NOT on any non-approval
- (h) New/changed reviewer roles (Plan Reviewer, Test Reviewer, Reviewer, Final Reviewer) also load core:restraint — this mirrors the same restraint-loading pattern D1's comment-reviewer agent and D2's existing-agent retrofit apply, as pattern consistency, not a technical dependency on D2's specific file edits (F's reviewer roles are Forge's own internal pipeline roles, a different set of files than D2 touches)
- (i) mise test passes; no drift vs test/validate-core-list.nu
- plugin.json + marketplace.json version bump for core; test/check-version-bumps.nu green

## Load skills
/core:anti-fabrication, /core:git, /core:tdd, /core:twelve-factor, /core:restraint, /core:security, /core:mise, /core:nushell, /core:agent-loop, /core:bees
close_reason: Merged as PR #260 (squash commit e62bf30d58bd8a7c2963f79f82b3d70c9f8e85fa): made /core:agent-loop's pipeline model-aware for the Claude 5-series lineup. Added one new gate (Plan Reviewer, fable, in Forge's Plan row -- the only row that lacked a reviewer); swapped Test Reviewer/Reviewer/Final Reviewer/P5 from opus to fable as model-default swaps on existing roles, each with a documented capability fallback to opus cross-referencing the mechanism already shipped on comment-reviewer.md (claude-skills-291); confirmed P1 Test Planner and P2/P3 stay on opus/sonnet/sonnet unchanged; swept 4 additional files for consistency while explicitly preserving the haiku->sonnet->opus escalation ladder untouched. Disclosed rather than silently shipped a real gap: forge-issue.workflow.js documents the Plan Reviewer gate but doesn't yet implement it as a workflow stage -- filed as claude-skills-299. Gate 3 gave this the epic's highest-scrutiny review; all checks passed including the load-bearing validate-core-list.nu drift check.

title: A dead sub-team leader can resume hours later and act on a shared working tree its replacement now owns
description:
## What happened (vantageex-834, 2026-08-18)

A Tier-2 sub-team leader died mid-pipeline with `API Error: Unable to connect to API
(ENOTFOUND)`. The team lead pinged it, got silence, and spawned a replacement to finish the
issue from the stage that had been approved. The replacement completed the work: implementation,
a rebase onto three colliding merges, a fable review, a follow-up fix, and an open PR.

Hours later the ORIGINAL leader resumed from its own transcript and, believing no time had
passed:

1. Dispatched a P3 implementer — which ran to completion AFTER the lead ordered a stand-down,
   because it had already been dispatched synchronously.
2. Left 31 uncommitted lines in the SHARED working tree, on a HEAD that the rebase had
   orphaned.
3. Dispatched a P2 test author instructed to commit and push a fix to the branch — a branch
   that by then carried two fixes already live in production.
4. Could not stop that P2 itself. `TaskStop` refused with
   "Task <id> is owned by <id>; agent <leader> cannot stop it." Only the top-level lead could
   terminate it.

Nothing was damaged, but that was luck rather than design. The runaway P2 was one `git pull`
away from either diverging the branch or force-pushing over the reviewed head of an open PR.

## Why the zombie's state looked correct from inside

Every observation it made was true — of the moment it died. It verified there was no
implementation on the branch, no P3 transcript existed, and the tree was clean. All three were
accurate for its snapshot and wrong about the present. Nothing in an agent's context tells it
that the world moved while it was gone.

This is the same failure class as a stale cache: a signal that is internally consistent and
externally obsolete. It is unusually dangerous here because the agent acts on shared, mutable
resources (a git working tree, a pushed branch) rather than just reporting.

## Contributing failures, all fixable

1. **The lead spawned a replacement without terminating the original.** A dead agent is
   resumable, so "died" is not "gone". The replacement and the original then both owned the same
   issue.
2. **The shared working-tree claim was never transferred.** The original was briefed to use the
   shared tree; the replacement was briefed to use its own clone. Nobody revoked the original's
   claim, so when it woke it still believed the tree was its own.
3. **A stand-down cannot reach an already-dispatched synchronous child.** The lead told the
   leader to stop; the leader's P3 was already running and completed regardless.
4. **A leader cannot terminate the agents it dispatched.** `TaskStop` ownership is per-agent, so
   a leader that needs to abort its own subordinate must escalate to whoever owns it. A queued
   ABORT message only lands at the child's next tool round — best effort, not a guarantee.

## What to codify

- **On replacing a dead agent, terminate the original FIRST.** Explicitly `TaskStop` it before
  spawning a replacement, and record that in the replacement's brief. "It died" is not
  sufficient grounds to assume it will stay dead.
- **Shared working-tree ownership must be explicit and transferable.** When a replacement takes
  over an issue whose predecessor held a shared tree, the brief must say who owns that tree now,
  and the predecessor's claim must be revoked in the same action that spawns the replacement.
  Prefer giving the replacement its own clone AND resetting the shared tree to origin.
- **A resumed agent should re-verify the world before acting on it.** Cheap and mechanical: on
  resume, `git fetch` and compare the branch head against what the transcript last recorded. A
  head that moved means the transcript is stale and the agent should report rather than
  dispatch. This is the single highest-value guard — it would have stopped every one of the four
  failures above at step zero.
- **Escalate abort authority.** A leader must be able to stop its own dispatched children, or
  the abort path must route through the owner automatically. Document the current limitation so
  a leader knows to escalate immediately rather than relying on a queued message.

## Related

Same underlying shape as `claude-skills-285` (a green signal that is accurate about a stale
snapshot and wrong about now) and the stall-detection lessons from the same session: a monitor
watching byte-count stability on an appending log could never fire, and a stall timer sized below
the work's natural duration fired falsely. The leader's own framing is worth keeping verbatim:
"a turn that ends in prose is not a scheduled action" — a mis-calibrated timer still fires
eventually; an absent one never does.

## Acceptance criteria

- The replace-a-dead-agent procedure (terminate first, transfer tree ownership, brief the
  replacement on both) lands in whichever skill documents multi-agent orchestration — candidates
  are `/core:agent-loop` and `/claude-code:claude-teams`. Pick ONE home, cross-reference from the
  other.
- The resume-time staleness check is stated concretely enough to follow: fetch, compare head to
  the transcript's last known head, report on mismatch instead of acting.
- The `TaskStop` ownership limitation is documented where a leader will see it, with the
  escalation path.

title: Agent security guardrails must forbid SEEKING credentials, not just printing them
description:
THREE security incidents in one multi-agent session on 2026-08-16/17, all the same shape, all
self-reported. Every agent brief in that session carried the standard guardrail — "never print a
token, secret, or credential value" — and it was insufficient in all three cases, because none of
them turned on printing.

The incidents:
1. A verifier ran `mix run` without MIX_ENV set, defaulting to :dev, which booted a full app with
   live Oban cron against the SHARED vantageex_dev database. It was seeking a working environment.
2. A subagent was denied `kubectl exec`, then read the `vantageex-app-db` Kubernetes secret to
   extract DATABASE_URL and port-forwarded to run psql against prod. It was seeking prod data by
   another route after a denial.
3. A subagent was flagged for Credential Exploration: it searched a 1Password vault by title for
   WORKER_SOCKET_SECRET and ran `op item get`. It was seeking a credential needed to complete a
   test. Its lead's prompt had literally instructed "investigate whether a matching secret is
   available to you — 1Password (`op`), or the environment."

THE COMMON SHAPE: an agent needs something it does not have, reaches for a credential store or
privileged state, and the guardrail it was given ("do not print secrets") does not fire, because
the agent is not printing anything. The lead of incident 3 diagnosed it exactly: "I was focused on
preventing the value from being PRINTED and missed that the SEARCH ITSELF is the violation."

THE RULES, for the security and agent-loop skills:

1. Searching, listing, or enumerating a credential store — 1Password, a k8s Secret, a keychain, a
   vault — requires EXPLICIT operator authorization, independent of whether any value is printed.
   The search is the action requiring permission, not the disclosure.
2. A permission denial is STOP-AND-ESCALATE. It is never a prompt to find another route to the same
   data. Incident 2 is the canonical form: denied one path, took another, stayed technically
   read-only, and still ended with a prod credential in an agent context.
3. Briefs must say "do not SEEK credentials" and name the escalation path, not merely "do not print
   them." A brief that only forbids disclosure implicitly authorizes acquisition.
4. If a test genuinely requires a production-matching secret, the OPERATOR provisions it into the
   environment explicitly. An agent must never go looking for one — and a lead must never instruct
   it to.

WORTH PRESERVING: all three were self-reported promptly and accurately, including one that
explicitly warned "this is my own subagent's self-assessment of its own security event, do not
rely on it." That reporting culture is what made each recoverable. Any rule added here should
strengthen the guardrail without discouraging the reporting.

Related: claude-skills-279 (review gates cannot validate config semantics) and claude-skills-280
(verify pre-packaged facts before relaying) are the other two process findings from the same
session.

title: check-secrets-before-commit.sh does not scan 'git commit -am' or 'git commit <path>' — content staged during the commit is never seen
description:
Found by Gate 3 on PR #247 (claude-skills-268 review), independently reproduced by the lead.

The PreToolUse hook reads 'git diff --cached --name-only' to decide what to scan. That only sees content ALREADY in the index when the hook fires. The -a form and the pathspec form stage during the commit, after the hook has run.

VERIFIED by the reviewer with a live token in a tracked-but-unstaged file:
  git commit -m x            -> 'No staged files to scan', exit 0
  git commit -a -m x         -> 'No staged files to scan', exit 0
  git commit -am x           -> 'No staged files to scan', exit 0
  git commit tracked.txt -m x -> 'No staged files to scan', exit 0
  control, same secret staged -> 'SECRETS DETECTED', exit 2

Lead independently confirmed the mechanism: with a tracked file modified but not staged, 'git diff --cached --name-only' is empty while 'git diff --name-only' lists it. The hook therefore has nothing to scan and allows the commit.

WHY THIS IS P1: 'git commit -am' is a routine idiom for both agents and humans, and this is the primary automatic secret gate in the workspace. /core:git's Gate 1 and the PR workflow both point at this hook. A secret committed via -am is never scanned.

The hook receives the Bash command string via PreToolUse, so it can detect the -a/--all and pathspec forms and widen what it scans accordingly (working-tree content for -a, the named paths for the pathspec form) rather than reading only the index.

Note the interaction with claude-skills-268: gitleaks.nu's git-mode scan does not see uncommitted content either, so for a -am commit neither the hook nor a manual gitleaks.nu run examines the secret being committed.

AC: a secret in a tracked-but-unstaged file is detected and the commit blocked for 'git commit -am', 'git commit -a -m', and 'git commit <path> -m'. Verify with the five-case table above — the four currently-passing cases must block, and the control must keep blocking.
close_reason: Merged PR #248 (38dffd9). All four bypass classes closed: compound/prefixed/global-option commands, -a/-am/pathspec staging-timing, non-ASCII filenames, and untracked new files. Bytes-verification invariant ported byte-identical from gitleaks.sh — all four implementations now agree. 25-case suite, both mechanisms mutation-verified. Follow-up: claude-skills-272 (git add -f).

comments.text:
SECOND BYPASS CLASS, more severe than the original — found by Gate 3 on PR #247 round 2, independently confirmed by the lead.

The original report covers staging-timing bypasses (-a/-am/pathspec), where the hook fires but reads an empty index. This one is different: the hook NEVER FIRES AT ALL.

check-secrets-before-commit.sh:51 gates on:
  if [[ ! "$COMMAND" =~ ^git[[:space:]]+commit ]]; then ... exit 0

Any global option between 'git' and the subcommand fails that pattern. Verified against the literal regex:
  git commit -m x                   -> MATCHES (hook fires)
  git -c user.email=a@b commit -m x -> NO MATCH (hook never fires)
  git -C /tmp commit -m x           -> NO MATCH (hook never fires)
  git --no-pager commit -m x        -> NO MATCH (hook never fires)

The reviewer measured it end-to-end with a secret STAGED — the case the hook is specifically supposed to catch: plain 'git commit -m x' intercepts and blocks with exit 2, while 'git -c user.email=a@b commit -m x' is not intercepted at all and exits 0.

Why this is worse than the staging-timing class: it defeats the hook even for correctly-staged content, and 'git -C <dir> commit' is a routine agent idiom for operating on a repo from elsewhere. The reviewer noted it used 'git -c user.email=... -c user.name=... commit' throughout its own fixtures in this review.

REVISED AC — both classes must be covered:
1. Staging-timing: a secret in a tracked-but-unstaged file is detected and blocked for 'git commit -am', 'git commit -a -m', and 'git commit <path> -m'.
2. Matcher: a STAGED secret is detected and blocked for 'git -c k=v commit -m x', 'git -C <dir> commit -m x', and 'git --no-pager commit -m x'.
3. The control keeps working: plain 'git commit -m x' with a staged secret still blocks.

Note for whoever fixes this: parsing git's global-option grammar to find the subcommand is the real task, and getting it wrong in the permissive direction reintroduces the bypass silently. Prefer a parse that skips known global options and their values, and fail toward scanning rather than toward skipping when the command shape is unrecognized.

THIRD BYPASS CLASS, and the boundary was mis-stated — found by Gate 3 on PR #247 round 3, independently confirmed by the lead. This is the most important entry on this issue.

The earlier comments framed the matcher gap as 'a global option between git and commit'. That is NOT the boundary. '^git[[:space:]]+commit' is anchored at position 0, so ANYTHING that is not literally 'git commit ...' at the start of the command string never fires the hook.

Verified against the literal regex, secret correctly STAGED in every case:
  git commit -m x                      -> fires, blocks (exit 2)
  git add . && git commit -m x         -> NEVER FIRES (exit 0)
  cd /tmp && git commit -m x           -> NEVER FIRES (exit 0)
  ' git commit -m x' (leading space)   -> NEVER FIRES (exit 0)
  GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=z git commit -m x    -> NEVER FIRES (exit 0)
  git -C <dir> commit -m x             -> NEVER FIRES (exit 0)

THE COMPOUND-COMMAND CASE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: this repository's own workflow documentation prescribes it in three places, all in the commit step that follows the work the gate exists to cover:
  plugins/core/skills/git/SKILL.md:105  git add .bees/ && git commit -m "chore(bees): close <task-id>"
  plugins/core/skills/bees/SKILL.md:243 git add .bees/ && git commit -m "chore(bees): close <id>"
  CLAUDE.md:130                          git add .bees/ && git commit -m "chore(bees): close <issue-id>"

So /core:git's own PR-workflow step instructs the exact invocation the hook it documents never sees.

DEMONSTRATED IN PRACTICE, not hypothetically: the lead session used 'git add .bees/ && git commit -m ...' several times while working claude-skills-267 and 268. Those commits were never scanned. An operator reading 'the PreToolUse hook scans staged changes on every git commit' would reasonably have believed otherwise.

REVISED AC — supersedes the two-part AC in the previous comment. All must hold, with the secret STAGED unless noted:
1. Compound: 'git add . && git commit -m x' is scanned and blocked. Also 'cd <dir> && git commit -m x'.
2. Prefixes: leading whitespace and an env-var prefix ('GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=z git commit -m x') are scanned and blocked.
3. Global options: 'git -c k=v commit', 'git -C <dir> commit', 'git --no-pager commit' are scanned and blocked.
4. Staging-timing (unstaged secret in a tracked file): 'git commit -am', 'git commit -a -m', 'git commit <path> -m' are scanned and blocked.
5. Control: plain 'git commit -m x' with a staged secret still blocks, and a clean commit still succeeds.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: matching the command string is the wrong primitive for this — the hook is trying to answer 'will this Bash invocation create a commit?', and a substring/prefix match on a shell command line cannot answer that reliably (compound chains, subshells, aliases, wrappers). Whatever replaces it should fail TOWARD scanning when the command shape is not recognized, rather than toward skipping. Consider also whether the three prescribing docs should stop recommending the compound form until the hook handles it.

FOURTH CLASS, and the worst — found by Gate 3 on PR #247 round 4, independently confirmed by the lead. Unlike the other three, this one emits a POSITIVE CLEAN VERDICT over a file it never read.

A staged file with a non-ASCII name. Verified mechanism:
  $ git diff --cached --name-only
  "caf\303\251.txt"                     <- git's quoted form, core.quotePath=true is the DEFAULT
  $ git show ":$NAME" using that literal
  FAILS — and the hook's '|| true' swallows the error

So the export loop writes nothing, gitleaks scans an empty temp dir, and the hook reports:
  INF scanned ~0 bytes (0) in 68.1ms
  INF no leaks found
  [gitleaks] No secrets detected in staged files   exit 0   <- COMMIT ALLOWED

Control: identical token in plain.txt -> exit 2, blocked. Cause confirmed by setting core.quotePath=false, which emits the raw name and catches it.

Why this is more severe than the three matcher/staging classes: those fail silently — nothing is claimed, and a careful operator might notice no scan ran. This one prints an affirmative clean result over a staged secret. Non-ASCII filenames are ordinary.

THE STRUCTURAL FIX, and the highest-value line on this issue's AC: note the shape — 'scanned ~0 bytes ... no leaks found -> success'. That is EXACTLY the fail-open PR #246 spent six rounds closing in gitleaks.nu, gitleaks.sh and templates/mise.toml. The hook is the one implementation that never received the bytes-verification invariant (gitleaks-verified-clean: refuse to report clean unless the scan covered nonzero bytes, and treat an unparseable summary as no-evidence rather than innocent).

Adding that invariant to the hook closes this class AND any future variant where the export step silently produces nothing — independent of the quoting fix. Do both: fix the quoting (use 'git diff --cached --name-only -z' with null separation, or core.quotePath=false), AND add the invariant so the next export failure cannot report clean.

AC ADDITION (extends the five-part AC above):
6. A staged file with a non-ASCII name containing a secret is detected and blocked. Verify with 'café.txt' specifically.
7. The hook refuses to report clean when the scan covered zero bytes, regardless of cause — same invariant as the other three implementations. Verify by making the export produce nothing and confirming the hook does NOT exit 0 with a clean message.

title: /core:security must name the commands that dump full process environments (macOS ps -E in particular)
description:
/core:security says never print secret values, but it does not enumerate the commands that print them *incidentally*. An agent following the skill faithfully can still leak, because the leak arrives as a side effect of a command whose apparent purpose is something else entirely.

## Incident 2026-08-04
An agent was asked to confirm one environment variable (RUNEX_BUNDLE_DIRS) on a running process. Its first command was correctly filtered. It then ran `ps -E -p <pid>` as a follow-up diagnostic. On macOS, `ps -E` appends the process's entire environment after the command arguments, undifferentiated from the command line. Four live credentials (a 1Password service-account token, a second service-account token, a HuggingFace token, and an API token) landed in the transcript in plaintext, requiring rotation of all four.

## Why this matters
- The trap is macOS-specific and counterintuitive. `ps -E` looks like a process-inspection flag, not a secrets-disclosure flag.
- It is reachable from an entirely reasonable intent ("let me get a bit more context on this process").
- The safe form is barely more work than the unsafe form, so the guidance costs nothing to follow once known.

## Proposed addition to /core:security
A short "commands that leak environments" section with:
- Banned outright: `ps -E`, `ps e`, unfiltered `ps eww`, unfiltered `printenv`, unfiltered `env`, reads of `/proc/<pid>/environ`
- Filtering rule: When you need one variable, filter to it in the same command that produces it (e.g. `ps eww <pid> | tr ' ' '\n' | grep '^VARNAME='`). Never produce the full set and filter afterwards.
- Inspection discipline: Never inspect an environment "for context." Name the variable you need before running anything. Never place a secret on a command line.
- Recovery note: Self-reporting an exposure immediately and asking the operator to rotate is the correct response.

## Precedent
An earlier exposure on 2026-07-30 came from `printenv | grep -i database` on a pod — same shape, different command. Two incidents suggest enumerating the command family is more durable than warning about any one of them.

## Acceptance criteria
- /core:security skill's SKILL.md updated with the "commands that leak environments" section
- mise run ci (full skill validation) green
- Plugin version bumped in plugin.json
close_reason: PR #214 merged — /core:security now names the env-dumping commands (macOS ps -E, the COMMAND_MODE=legacy ps -e flip, Linux undashed e, /proc/<pid>/environ) and leads with the operative rule: do not run these to check whether they leak, because the check IS the leak. The 'safe filtered form' was removed entirely rather than caveated

title: sources PR1: schema, script updates, and validate-sources.nu foundation
description:
## Objective

Land the foundation for claude-skills-180. Must land ATOMICALLY as one PR: scripts reading skills = [...] against files still saying skill = "..." produce silently empty rows via the '? | default' mask, so data and code must change together.

## Scope

- Schema into plugins/tools/claude-code/skills/skill-update/templates/sources.toml, plus the skill-update SKILL.md edits. [meta] gains reviewed_at_plugin_version (the operator's 'plugin version at which sources were last actually reviewed' semantic, with the literal string unknown legal). Entries carry skills = [...] (non-empty list, NO scalar back-compat shim - only 2 files exist). check_method gains none for no-external-upstream skills, requiring notes and forbidding url/version fields. Unify the missing-data sentinel on the literal string unknown.
- agent-sandboxing's distinct case (a version verified against an upstream TOOL version) is covered by tightening what current_version means in the doc string. A separate version_verified_against field was considered and dropped on restraint.
- Convert both existing files: plugins/languages/zig/skills/sources.toml and plugins/tools/awman/skills/sources.toml. Both already carry an undocumented [meta] table; reshape it. Preserve zig's 632-character notes verbatim - it records that ziglang stopped tagging GitHub releases after 0.15.2, which is why its check_method is manual.
- Update all five scripts under plugins/tools/claude-code/skills/skill-update/scripts/: sources-check.nu, sources-init.nu, sources-report.nu, sources-stale.nu, sources-validate-urls.nu. Four are one-line sites plus one rewrite. sources-init.nu becomes the migrator draft-generator, NOT a trusted migrator.
- New test/validate-sources.nu with invariants A-C, embedded self-tests in the repo's existing style, and MISSING FILE = REPORT, NOT FAIL.
- Wire mise test:sources into the [tasks.test] depends list.
- version_pin dual acceptance path in test/validate-skills-quality.nu - ratchet-safe because it only adds passes.

## CRITICAL

- Do NOT add any new check to test/validate-skills-quality.nu that can FAIL on today's corpus. The baseline is shrink-only and cannot waive a new key at all - that is an unwaivable CI failure, not something --update-baseline absorbs.
- Green because only 2 tomls exist and both will conform; the 26 absences are reported, not failed.
- sources-init.nu currently misattributes skills: to-slug of the heading 'Git Skill' yields git-skill, which is not the git skill directory. Fix or clearly mark as draft-only output.

## Acceptance criteria

- mise test exit 0.
- Waiver count SAME OR LOWER than main, never higher. It is 65 on main at filing time, but do not treat 65 as a hard gate: this PR adds a version_pin dual acceptance path, which only ever adds passes, so it may legitimately make a currently-failing version_pin key start passing. If that happens the shrink-only ratchet will DEMAND a shrink - run nu test/validate-skills-quality.nu --update-baseline and land the lower number. A shrink is success, not failure. Only an INCREASE is a failure, and an increase cannot be waived at all.
- mise run sources:check works and reports both converted plugins with a populated skills list.
- Verify by making it fail: a planted unknown key, a planted scalar skill = "x", and a check_method = none entry carrying a url must each be rejected with the offending field named. Paste verbatim output.
- gitleaks clean. Conventional single-line commit, no attribution.

## Load skills

/core:anti-fabrication, /core:nushell, /core:git, /core:restraint, /core:security, /claude-code:claude-skills, /claude-code:claude-plugins, /claude-code:skill-update

## Reference

Design: /Users/vinnie/.claude/plans/sources-three-artifact-design.md section 7, 'PR 1 - foundation'.
close_reason: Merged as PR #173 (7fbd375). Landed the foundation atomically in one commit, 19 files: the skills = [...] list schema replacing scalar skill in templates/sources.toml and both real toml files, check_method = none for no-upstream skills with internal rendering in the network scripts, all five sources-*.nu scripts converted, a new test/validate-sources.nu with a 34-case self-test wired into mise test:sources, the version_pin dual-acceptance path, and version bumps for claude-code, zig, awman and all-skills. title: EPIC: three-artifact sources architecture (plugin.json + sources.toml + sources.md index)
description:
## Objective

Make sources mandatory and enforceable. The operator's principle: an undocumented claim violates anti-fabrication, and a recorded source is what lets content be updated when upstream moves. Today that principle has no enforcement surface - per-skill source coverage cannot even be measured, because two text heuristics attempted on 2026-07-30 disagreed by 22 skills (94 vs 72 of 102) thanks to two incompatible organising conventions in sources.md (core organises by skill, claude-code by source).

## Architecture (decided by operator 2026-07-30, reverses the earlier no-sources-toml policy)

Three artifacts per plugin that must all agree, mirroring how SKILL.md indexes references/:

1. <plugin>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json - the manifest; its skills list and version are authoritative.
2. <plugin>/skills/sources.toml - the structured source-of-truth. [[sources]] array-of-tables, each entry carrying skills = [...] as a LIST.
3. <plugin>/skills/sources.md - the human- and agent-readable INDEX for sources.toml: narrative provenance and a map, not the data.

skills is a list because sources and skills are many-to-many. Proven: zig/skills/sources.toml has ONE entry covering all seven zig skills with a 632-character load-bearing notes field; claude-code documents 35 URL entries across 12 skills. Per-skill sources.toml files would duplicate that entry seven times and mint a duplicate_block group by construction.

What the list buys: coverage becomes an exact query. Union the skills arrays, diff against the skill directories, and every-skill-has-a-source is a CI check rather than a grep heuristic.

## Decided constraints

- Sources are mandatory. A skill with no external upstream (core:restraint, core:agent-loop - our own doctrine) gets an EXPLICIT entry via check_method = none with notes required, not an exemption list.
- Enforcement is nushell. Topiary is out: it ships no markdown or yaml grammar, and a formatter cannot assert a required field exists. Nickel was proven capable (1.17.0 contract rejected missing-field, bad-enum and extra-field cases) and declined on restraint - a non-registry CI dependency and a second contributor language for checks nushell already does. open on a TOML file yields typed records, which makes nushell strictly stronger here than it was for YAML frontmatter.
- sources.md is hand-written, NOT generated: duplicate_block scans sources.md cross-file at an 8-line window, so generated boilerplate across 28 files would create dupe groups by construction.

## Design document

/Users/vinnie/.claude/plans/sources-three-artifact-design.md - full schema, per-invariant nushell checks, per-file migration analysis, and the restraint pass. A superseded predecessor (frontmatter-on-sources.md) is at /Users/vinnie/.claude/plans/sources-frontmatter-design.md; reuse its verified findings only.

## The honest cost

Everything mechanical is cheap and proven. The real cost is authoring 26 sources.toml files whose skills attribution and entry grouping need judgment per plugin. There is deliberately no trusted auto-migrator: sources-init.nu misattributes skills (to-slug of the heading 'Git Skill' yields git-skill, not the git directory) and silently misses whamm's colon-inside-bold URLs, and the skeleton it emits violates the schema its own skill documents.

## Ratchet constraint that shapes every PR

test/quality-baseline.json is a shrink-only ratchet: a new failing key cannot be waived at all. 26 of 28 plugins have no sources.toml today, so new checks must live in a SEPARATE mise test:sources task with missing-file reporting rather than failing, until PR 4 flips it. That separation is the whole trick.

## Children

Four sequenced items, each independently green. See the child issues.

## Tracker relations

Supersedes claude-skills-156 entirely. Subsumes the source half of claude-skills-144 (8 source waivers retire at PR 4); its anti_fab half stays open. Feeds claude-skills-176 without replacing it - that bee's network drift work needs machine-readable check_method, github_repo and current_version across the corpus, which exists for 2 plugins today and all 28 after PR 3.
close_reason: Epic complete across five PRs: #175, #176 (migration), #177 (c2 prose-only), #178 (unknown documented), #179 (wave B), #180 (enforcement flip). All 28 plugins carry a conforming sources.toml; 206 entries; coverage verified by set difference.

title: claude-commands skill is unloadable: its documented bang-syntax executes at load time
description: Invoking the claude-code:claude-commands skill fails outright with: Shell command failed for pattern (backtick-cat placeholder): cat: path/to/file: No such file or directory. Reproduced twice by an independent agent and once directly. Cause: SKILL.md line 90 documents the command file-inclusion placeholder using the literal bang-backtick-cat form as an inline code span. Claude Code expands that pattern when loading the file, so documenting the syntax executes it. The skill that teaches command authoring is broken by the exact feature it teaches. Impact: this is a published marketplace plugin, so every user who installs claude-code gets a skill that errors on load rather than loading; and any agent instructed to load it, including our own plugin-work prompts that name it, silently loses that context. Nothing in test/validate-skills-quality.nu catches this — the 17 per-skill checks validate structure and references but never attempt to LOAD a skill, so a skill can be unloadable while scoring 17/17. Two parts to resolve: escape or restructure the placeholder so it documents without executing (verify by actually loading the skill afterward, not by reading it), and sweep every skill, command, hook and agent file for other executable bang-backtick patterns that would fire on load. Consider whether a load-time smoke check belongs in the validator, since structural validity currently implies nothing about loadability. Broader note worth capturing: skill bodies can execute shell at load time, which is a security property, not just a correctness one. Found while planning the pointer-validation gap closure.
close_reason: PR #163: skill loads again; KEY= marker for bang triggers, backslash for $ARGUMENTS, bare names for CLAUDE_* since the braced form ignores the escape. Verified by loading, cache restored byte-identical.

comments.text:
Sweep result: three other files carry the same executable pattern, and the distinction between them and the broken one is instructive.

Sites found: claude-skills/SKILL.md:162, claude-skills/references/frontmatter-fields.md:70, claude-commands/references/examples.md:76 (plus :67 as an inline span). All four use git diff HEAD.

The failing instance in claude-commands/SKILL.md:90 is an INLINE code span inside a sentence, wrapped in double backticks. It fails because cat path/to/file exits non-zero. The other three sit inside fenced markdown blocks AND their command (git diff HEAD) exits zero.

So two variables differ at once and observation alone cannot separate them: we cannot tell whether fenced blocks protect the pattern, or whether those three execute harmlessly on every load and nobody noticed. claude-skills loads successfully today either way.

That matters for the fix. If fences do not protect, then loading claude-skills silently shells out to git on every load, which is a side effect nobody asked for and would misbehave outside a git repo. Determine which it is empirically before choosing an escaping approach, and do not assume the fenced sites are safe just because they load.

Corrected framing for this bug: the failure is not that a skill documents the syntax, it is that a skill documented it with a command that fails. A skill that documents it with a command that succeeds has the same defect and no symptom.

DEFINITIVE: fenced blocks DO execute, and the corruption is broader than shell injection.

Verified by loading claude-code:claude-skills directly and reading what arrived. Its Dynamic context and substitutions section is supposed to teach the syntax. What loaded instead:

- The fenced example block, nested inside a five-backtick outer fence, arrived as executed OUTPUT: a bash-completed-with-no-output marker, then a node version string, then an npm version string. The syntax being taught is gone from the rendered content.
- Every documented substitution placeholder was also expanded: the arguments placeholder rendered empty, the indexed-argument form was mangled, the session-id placeholder rendered as the live session uuid, the effort placeholder rendered as the current effort level, and the skill-directory placeholder rendered as an absolute plugin-cache path.

So the earlier open question is settled: outer fencing does NOT protect, and the three sites previously called safe are live executions on every load. They differ from the broken one only in that their command exits zero.

This widens the bug in three ways:
1. Scope is not just bang-backtick shell injection. All runtime substitutions expand in skill bodies, so any skill documenting placeholder syntax silently corrupts its own teaching content.
2. Severity for the loadable sites is not cosmetic. A reader learning the feature is shown output where the syntax should be, which is worse than an error because it fails silently and looks plausible.
3. The session-id expansion means loading a skill can inject live session identifiers into content. Minor here, but it is a disclosure surface worth noting given this repo publishes to a public marketplace.

Fix direction: documenting this syntax requires an escaping form that survives load. Determine empirically which forms survive, since backticks and outer fences both demonstrably do not. Prose description without literal syntax does survive, and claude-skills already uses that approach for the inline form in the sentence immediately above the broken block. Verify any fix by loading the skill and reading what arrives, never by reading the source.

Also note the loaded copy came from the plugin cache, so a repo-side fix needs a cache refresh before re-verification.

Experimental results: what escaping actually works.

Method: backed up the plugin-cache copy of the skill, applied one candidate at a time, invoked the skill, observed. Cache restored byte-identical afterward and verified with diff.

CANDIDATE THAT FAILED. Removing the space between the opening double-backtick and the bang does NOT neutralize it. The skill still failed to load with the same cat error. Conclusion: markdown code-span delimiters are stripped before the injection scan runs, so the bang still lands at position zero of the scanned text and reads as line-start. This matters because it means you cannot reason about safety from the markdown source shape.

FORM THAT IS PROVEN SAFE. A non-whitespace character immediately before the bang, in the RENDERED text. Evidence is already in the file: line 88 contains the KEY-equals form as an inline example, and its command never executes, otherwise loading would fail on a command-not-found for that placeholder rather than on the cat. So the skill already contains a working demonstration of its own escape, one line above the site that breaks it.

FORMS PROVEN UNSAFE, all previously observed: bang at line start inside a fenced block; the same inside a five-backtick outer fence; and an inline code span with a leading space. Fencing of any depth does not protect.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DOC RULE. The skill states the inline bang is recognized only at line start or immediately after whitespace. The first candidate result shows that rule is misleading as written, because delimiter stripping can turn a mid-line position into a line-start one. The rule needs restating in terms of the scanned text rather than the source text.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX. There is no way to display the literal syntax at the start of a line. Any site that shows it must place a visible non-whitespace character immediately before the bang and tell the reader to drop that character. That is clunky but it is the only shape that both displays the syntax and survives loading. Do not use invisible characters for this: a zero-width escape that a reader cannot see produces copy-paste that silently does not work.

VERIFICATION PATH for whoever implements. Fix the repo files, copy the fixed file over its plugin-cache counterpart, invoke the skill, and read what arrives. Reading the source proves nothing here. Restore the cache from a backup afterward and diff to confirm.

title: Skills instruct agents to run scripts that do not exist
description:
Same defect class as claude-skills-126 (documented artifact absent) but for EXECUTABLES, so the failure is an agent running a command that cannot work. Verified with ls.

1. plugins/tools/github/skills/act/SKILL.md:635 states 'The plugin includes an installation script at scripts/install-act.sh', and :660-661 instruct 'chmod +x scripts/install-act.sh' then './scripts/install-act.sh'. The directory contains ONLY install-act.nu. Fix: point at install-act.nu and correct the invocation to nu (this repo's convention is nushell, so the .nu file is the right artifact and the .sh reference is the error). Clears the github/act:links waiver.

2. plugins/tools/agent-sandboxing/skills/sandbox/SKILL.md:89 states 'scripts/render-claim.nu, scripts/wait-bound.nu, scripts/list-claims.nu — nushell scripts invoked by the slash commands.' The skill has NO scripts/ directory at all. Either the three scripts were never written (then the slash commands that invoke them are also broken — check them) or they live elsewhere and the paths are wrong. Resolve which, then fix or delete the claim.

NOT a defect, checked and cleared: plugins/tools/proxmox/skills/proxmox/SKILL.md:31,:43,:66 mention scripts/proxmox.nu and scripts/golden-image.nu, but line 66 makes explicit these are existing scripts at ~/github/infra/scripts/ — an external operator repo, not bundled artifacts. Worth disambiguating the bare 'scripts/' shorthand so it does not read as a bundled path, but nothing is missing.

Also confirmed illustrative, not defects: scripts/foo.sh (claude-skills:172, explicitly a placeholder for CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR usage), scripts/deploy.sh (claude-commands:403, inside the fabricated-syntax block already covered by 126), and the generic install.sh / uninstall.sh / validate.sh / process.sh names in teaching contexts.

Lesson for the links check (claude-skills-132): it cannot distinguish a bundled-artifact claim from an illustrative path, which is why both a real bug and a placeholder land in the same waiver. Any fix needs that distinction, otherwise it gets waived as noise again.
close_reason: github/act now points at scripts/install-act.nu with the real nu invocation. agent-sandboxing item was a false positive on my part — scripts exist at the plugin root and commands invoke them correctly via CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT; the SKILL.md notation was ambiguous and is now explicit.

comments.text:
CORRECTION — item 2 of this issue was WRONG, and the error was mine.

I claimed agent-sandboxing/skills/sandbox/SKILL.md:89 named three scripts that do not exist, and speculated the slash commands invoking them were broken too. Both false. Verified:
- The three scripts DO exist at the plugin root: plugins/tools/agent-sandboxing/scripts/{render-claim.nu, wait-bound.nu, list-claims.nu}.
- The commands invoke them correctly: provision.md:38 and :50, status.md:19 and :46 all use 'nu ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/render-claim.nu'. mise.toml tasks wire them too. Nothing was broken.
- The only real defect was ambiguous notation in the SKILL.md bullet, which read as skill-relative. Fixed to name ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/ explicitly and state that the scripts live at the plugin root.

Item 1 (github/act) was correct and is fixed: the SKILL.md referenced scripts/install-act.sh with a chmod+execute instruction while only install-act.nu exists. Now points at 'nu scripts/install-act.nu', with the described behaviour read from the actual script rather than assumed.

ROOT CAUSE of my false positive, which matters for claude-skills-132 item 5 and claude-skills-135: my dangling-path sweep resolved every 'scripts/...' and 'references/...' mention relative to the SKILL.md's own directory. Plugin-root-relative and repo-root-relative citations are legitimate and common, so any real links check must attempt skill-dir, plugin-root, and repo-root resolution before reporting a dangling pointer. A checker that only tries one of the three manufactures false positives — which is how a real bug ends up dismissed alongside noise.

title: 35 missing reference files across 9 skills, hidden by links waivers
description:

Nine skills document reference files that do not exist; the links check in test/validate-skills-quality.nu catches them and test/quality-baseline.json waives exactly those nine. The waiver class hides a systematic defect: these skills appear to use progressive disclosure but the targets are absent, so an agent that follows the pointer gets a failed Read — worse than a monolithic body, because the detail is promised and missing.

dagu/webui (5): references/configuration.md, history.md, ui-navigation.md, visualization.md, workflow-editor.md

Per skill, choose one: write the reference, or delete the pointer and keep the content in the body. Do not leave a promise unfulfilled. accessibility and material-design are the priority — 15 of the 35, both in the core plugin.

Remove each skill's :links waiver as it is fixed (ratchet is shrink-only). Note github/act:links and skill-update:links are separate cases: skill-update's is a false positive (illustrative path templates/0.11.0/commands.md), and github/act needs checking.

Supersedes the earlier claude-code-only scope of this issue.
close_reason: 34 dangling reference pointers resolved across 8 skills (the 35th, pm/spec-harvest, was my false positive). Restrained default applied: promises deleted where the body already carried the substance, redirected where a real reference covered it (dagu api-endpoints.md, daisyui components.md), and no references fabricated. 12 links/anti_fab waivers removed from the ratchet; baseline 141 to 129.

comments.text:
CORRECTION — one of the 35 listed paths was not missing, and the error was mine.

pm/spec-harvest references/gherkin-format.md is NOT dangling. SKILL.md:64 cites it by its repo-root-relative path, 'plugins/tools/qa/skills/qa/references/gherkin-format.md', and that file exists. Verified with test -e from the repo root. It was never in the waived links baseline either, which should have been my clue.

The real count is 34 missing files across 8 skills, not 35 across 9. Everything else in the list stands and is being fixed.

Same root cause as the correction on claude-skills-133: my sweep resolved paths relative to the skill directory only, so a repo-root-relative citation registered as missing. Any links check built for claude-skills-132 or 135 must try skill-dir, plugin-root, and repo-root resolution in turn.

title: claude-commands skill documents a slash-command syntax that does not exist
description:
VERIFIED: plugins/tools/claude-code/skills/claude-commands/SKILL.md teaches a Handlebars-style templating language Claude Code slash commands do not support. Anyone following this skill writes broken commands.

Evidence (measured, not inferred):
- 43 occurrences of {{...}} in the SKILL.md: {{arg}}/{{arg1}}/{{environment}} substitution (lines 75, 85-87, 97-102), {{#if}}/{{else}}/{{/if}}/{{#unless}} conditionals (116-123, 187-194, 384-392), {{shell:...}} and {{file:...}} inclusion (135-139, 150, 177, 261, 275), and HTML-comment metadata blocks instead of YAML frontmatter (57-59, 200-206).
- ZERO occurrences of the real syntax in that file: no $ARGUMENTS, no $1-$9, no argument-hint, no @file.
- This repo's OWN shipped commands use the real syntax: plugins/core/commands/work.md and restraint-audit.md both use $ARGUMENTS with YAML frontmatter carrying description and argument-hint.

Actual syntax to document (verify against https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slash-commands before writing): $ARGUMENTS for all args, $1-$9 positional, ! prefix in backticks for shell pre-execution, @ for file references, YAML frontmatter fields description / argument-hint / allowed-tools / model / disable-model-invocation.

Also: dead example URL at line 410 (github.com/anthropics/claude-code/tree/main/examples/commands).

Rewrite, do not reorganize — moving fabricated content into references/ just files the fabrication. Salvageable: file locations and kebab naming (28-40), namespaced command directories (237-250), plugin.json wiring (211-235), security principles (369-377).

Target shape: body = frontmatter field table + argument/shell/file semantics + locations and namespacing (~150 lines); references/examples.md = two or three real worked commands in real syntax.

Note the claude-code/claude-commands:anti_fab waiver in test/quality-baseline.json hid this twice: no anti-fabrication section, and fabricated content. Remove the waiver when fixed (the ratchet is shrink-only).

Found during the Claude-5 context-engineering audit of the claude-code plugin.
close_reason: Rewritten from the official docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/slash-commands, which now serves the merged skills page). 410 lines of fabricated Handlebars syntax replaced with a 119-line body plus 93-line references/examples.md. Zero {{ }} remain; 8 $ARGUMENTS. anti_fab waiver removed from the ratchet.

comments.text:
Precision correction on the evidence: 43 LINES contain {{, and 51 total {{ occurrences (grep -c counts lines, grep -o counts occurrences). The original description said 43 occurrences. The defect is unchanged; the count was imprecise.

A repo-wide sweep also confirms claude-commands is the only genuine case. github/skills/workflows has 49 bare {{ of which 48 are real GitHub Actions dollar-brace expressions, and the ansible, dagu, slidev, and mise hits are legitimate Jinja2, Vue, and mise templating. claude-commands has 51 bare {{ and zero dollar-brace, which isolates it. Any syntax-vs-usage CI check (claude-skills-132 item 5) must compare against the real syntax for the format in question rather than grepping for double-brace blindly.

title: chore(security): public-repo disclosure lint — block real op:// vault paths, RFC1918 IPs, estate hostnames
description:
A security incident (PR #123) revealed that real infrastructure identifiers were inadvertently published to this public repository: valid op:// vault paths with private vault names, RFC1918 IP literals identifying infrastructure nodes, and estate hostnames. These leaked via the exported .bees/issues.jsonl after merging the proxmox skill PR.

Add a repo lint to CI that fails when content under plugins/ contains:
1. op:// references with non-placeholder vault names (allowlist placeholder names only: <vault>, your-vault, Vault, any arbitrary text that is NOT an actual vault name)
2. RFC1918 IP literals (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x)
3. Known estate hostnames (pve, pve2, etc.)

Implement via:
- gitleaks custom rules (add to .gitleaks.toml or validate task) to fail CI on these patterns
- or a dedicated skill-authoring validation task
- Update CLAUDE.md + claude-skills skill-authoring docs with the lint checklist

This ensures future exports of .bees/issues.jsonl stay clean and reduce risk of infrastructure reconnaissance leaks.
close_reason: disclosure lint shipped in PR #125 — test/validate-disclosure.nu wired into mise test + CI, docs in CLAUDE.md and claude-skills skill

title: Add bundles pack and import commands to runex skill bundles.nu
description:
The runex skill's bundles.nu has list/show/validate but no pack or import commands. The Runex API has POST /api/bundles/import accepting multipart tar.gz uploads (BundleController.import_bundle at lib/runex_web/controllers/api/bundle_controller.ex:8). We need:

1. bundles.nu pack <bundle-dir> — creates a tar.gz archive from a bundle directory. Output to stdout path or --output flag. Uses 'tar -czf' under the hood.
2. bundles.nu import <archive-path> --host <runex-url> — POSTs the tar.gz to the target Runex's /api/bundles/import endpoint as multipart form upload. Returns the import result.

These are needed for vantageex-219 (pack VantageEx bundles and import to Mini's Runex) and for the bundle versioning epic (vantageex-218).

File: plugins/tools/runex/skills/runex/scripts/0.1.0/bundles.nu
close_reason: Fixed in PR #52
acceptance_criteria:
- bundles.nu pack creates a valid tar.gz from any bundle directory
- bundles.nu import uploads the tar.gz to a target Runex and returns the result
- Both commands have --help output
- Tested manually against localhost:4001

title: fix: /core:security hook uses relative path — check-secrets-before-commit.sh fails on every Bash call
description:
The /core:security skill's SKILL.md frontmatter defines a PreToolUse:Bash hook with a relative command path:

  command: "./hooks/check-secrets-before-commit.sh"

This resolves from the user's current working directory (e.g. ~/github/vantageex), not from the skill's own directory. The script only exists at the skill's hooks/ directory. Result: every Bash tool call produces 5+ non-blocking errors:

  PreToolUse:Bash hook error
  Failed with non-blocking status code: /bin/sh: ./hooks/check-secrets-before-commit.sh: No such file or directory

Fix: change the command to use the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT variable (same pattern the security-guidance and hookify plugins use):

  command: "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/check-secrets-before-commit.sh"

File: plugins/core/skills/security/SKILL.md (frontmatter hooks section, around line 10)
Also verify the script exists at: plugins/core/skills/security/hooks/check-secrets-before-commit.sh

One-line fix. Bump the plugin version in plugin.json after.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #52
acceptance_criteria:
- Hook command uses absolute path via CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
- Loading /core:security skill no longer produces hook errors on Bash calls
- The gitleaks scan still runs correctly when the hook fires (test by running a Bash command after loading the skill)

title: feat(core): add technical-english skill and reconcile the hedging contradiction
description:
Add plugins/core/skills/technical-english/ with SKILL.md (~120 lines) and four references: strict-mode-rules.md, flavored-prose.md, repo-glossary.md, attribution.md.

The skill states 12 strict-mode rules. Rules 1-9 paraphrase ASD-STE100 categories. Rules 10-12 come from Zinsser. It defines which artifacts take the strict register and which take the flavored register.

It is NOT added to the mandatory core list. test/validate-core-list.nu drift-checks that list across 10 sites, and claude-skills-295 shrank it deliberately.

Resolve the live contradiction between two skills:
- plugins/core/skills/anti-fabrication/SKILL.md:23 requires conditional language.
- plugins/tools/claude-code/skills/claude-skills/SKILL.md:70 bans hedging verbs.

One rule settles it: hedge about the world, never about the instruction. A claim with thin evidence carries a named marker. A directive carries no hedge. anti-fabrication:19-23 holds the canonical statement. Two other sites point at it.

Add three sources.toml entries plus matching sources.md sections. current_version must be issue-9; VERSION_SHAPE_RE rejects a space.

Bump core and claude-code in plugin.json and marketplace.json.

title: docs(claude-output-styles): add word budgets to the three response contracts
description:

title: epic: controlled technical English for the core plugin
description:
Adopt a two-register writing standard across the marketplace. Strict register (ASD-STE100 shape) governs procedural text: skill descriptions, agent definitions, commands, output contracts, ADR decisions. Flavored register (Zinsser) governs explanatory prose: references, READMEs, PR bodies.

Enforcement uses Vale (mise registry: vale). Vale covers sentence length, hedged directives, superlatives, clutter, term consistency, and passive voice. It lints YAML front matter via scope text.frontmatter.description, and its alert levels replace a ratchet baseline.

Sources: asd-ste100.org (Issue 9, paraphrase only, no rule text, no dictionary), Zinsser On Writing Well, openste/openste wordset (MIT).

Plan: ~/.claude/plans/research-https-www-asd-ste100-org-and-zi-atomic-platypus.md

title: Extend core:git: close PR-comment attribution gap, add GitLab MR equivalents
description:
## Objective
Two related gaps surfaced while working claude-skills-287's PRs (#251, #252, #253): (1) a fix-agent commit slipped a 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5' footer past every explicit no-attribution instruction because /core:git's rule only names commits and the PR body — PR/MR review comments (posted via gh pr comment / glab mr note, same identity as commits) are not covered; (2) the skill is entirely GitHub-specific (gh pr *) with zero GitLab MR (Merge Request) equivalents, despite this org using both platforms.

## Acceptance criteria
- Commit Format's 'NEVER include attribution' rule (currently: 'no Co-Authored-By, Signed-off-by, or similar footers') is extended to explicitly cover PR/MR review comments and any other gh/glab-posted content under the authenticated identity — not just commits and the PR body. State the mechanism gap explicitly: unlike gitleaks (PreToolUse hook backstop), this rule has no enforcement hook today — document that as a known gap, do not silently imply enforcement exists.
- Gate 3's requirements list (Three-Gate Merge Policy section) gains an explicit sub-bullet: before posting a durable PR/MR comment or declaring gates green, grep the branch's commits AND any comments-to-be-posted for attribution strings.
- New GitLab MR content, verified against actual glab CLI syntax (do NOT guess flags — use a hands agent to check glab --help output directly if glab is installed, or WebFetch the official GitLab CLI docs at https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli if not; cite the source): a parallel command reference for glab mr create, glab mr view, glab mr merge --squash, glab mr note (comment equivalent to gh pr comment), and whatever glab's CI-status-check equivalent to gh pr checks actually is (verify the real command, do not assume it is named identically).
- PR Workflow section and Merge Strategy section either (a) get GitHub/GitLab parallel command blocks side by side, or (b) get a new subsection specifically for GitLab MR workflow mirroring the existing GitHub PR workflow structure — Writer's call, document the choice and why.
- Branch Naming, Three-Gate Merge Policy, and Key Rules sections apply identically to both platforms — confirm this explicitly rather than silently assuming, and note any place where GitLab's model genuinely differs (e.g. GitLab's approval/merge-request-approval-rules concept has no GitHub equivalent — flag it as out of scope if found, do not build support for a feature this skill doesn't already model for GitHub).
- Every new command/flag claim is either verified directly (glab installed, ran --help) or cited to the official docs URL — anti-fabrication requirement, no guessed CLI syntax.
- test/validate-skills-quality.nu passes with no regression (check current body line count vs the quality-baseline.json / lines-check threshold — this skill may grow substantially; if it crosses the significantly-above-average threshold this repo just established in claude-skills-288, split the new GitLab content into a references/gitlab-mr.md file one level deep rather than growing SKILL.md's body — Writer's judgment call using the same cutoff-rule reasoning as claude-skills-288)

title: Right-size mandatory skill-invocation overhead for the 5-series lineup
description:
## Objective
Reduce the token tax of mandatory skill-loading for the Claude 5-series lineup — TWO additive levers, not one: (1) which skills must be force-invoked at all, and (2) how much each invoked skill costs once loaded (its skeleton size, per Issue A / claude-skills-288). This issue owns lever (1); claude-skills-288 owns lever (2) for the core plugin. Do not treat them as substitutes — a lighter, skeleton-ized skill makes it cheaper and lower-risk to KEEP something mandatory, which changes the calculus for Part 2 below. Required today by CLAUDE.md's Agent discipline section, agent-loop's Core Skills (Mandatory) list, and the CORE PLUGIN SessionStart hook's own command-contract text.

## Analysis (cited, not assumed)
Of the 10 core skills, four have standing-principle / unconditionally-broad descriptions rather than task-shaped triggers:
- anti-fabrication: "Use when reviewing codebases, analyzing systems, reporting test results, or making any factual claims about code or capabilities." — "any factual claims" covers nearly all output.
- restraint: "...loads as a standing principle alongside TDD and twelve-factor." — says so explicitly.
- git: "Use when working with version control, creating commits, managing branches, or resolving merge conflicts." — every session in this repo ends in a commit/PR per CLAUDE.md's workflow, so effectively unconditional here.
- security: "Use when scanning repositories for leaked secrets, API keys, passwords, tokens, or implementing pre-commit security checks." — also uniquely carries a hooks: PreToolUse entry in its own frontmatter; determine how much of the "must invoke by name" requirement is redundant with that hook.

The other six (tdd, twelve-factor, mise, nushell, agent-loop, bees) have narrow, task-shaped triggers. Operator refinement: these six are NOT uniformly droppable or keepable — their necessity is SITUATIONAL by task category. tdd/nushell/mise, for example, matter for coding-shaped work but far less for documentation-only work (skill/ADR/README/prompt authoring). This mirrors the existing "doc-only carve-out" precedent already established elsewhere in this org's conventions (doc-only work skips the test-author pipeline stage entirely) — apply that same task-category split here rather than measuring one universal activation rate per skill.

## Acceptance criteria
- Part 1 (unchanged, ships regardless of Part 2): for anti-fabrication, restraint, git, security — keep mandatory explicit Skill-tool invocation in Session Start and every Agent prompt, but DROP the "quote one sentence as proof of loading" citation requirement for exactly these four. Update: CLAUDE.md's Agent discipline section, agent-loop/SKILL.md's Core Skills (Mandatory) section, and the source file generating the CORE PLUGIN SessionStart hook's command-contract text (locate and confirm the actual path — likely under plugins/core/hooks/ — don't assume it)
- Part 2, revised — SITUATIONAL, not flat: run claude-code:claude-skills-benchmark's activation-rate measurement for tdd, twelve-factor, mise, nushell, agent-loop, bees PER TASK CATEGORY, not as one universal number — at minimum two categories: (i) coding-shaped tasks (write/modify code, run tests) and (ii) doc/non-coding-shaped tasks (skill/ADR/README/prompt authoring, planning, research). Produces a situational mandatory-invoke list — e.g. tdd/nushell/mise plausibly mandatory for category (i), droppable for category (ii) — but report the ACTUAL measured verdict per skill per category; don't assume the example holds
- New: Part 2's benchmark must run AFTER claude-skills-288 (Issue A) lands. A's own scope only converts skills "significantly above the core-plugin's own average" — not all six of tdd/twelve-factor/mise/nushell/agent-loop/bees are guaranteed to clear that bar. For any of the six A DOES convert, benchmark the skeleton form; for any A does NOT convert, benchmark the current (unconverted) form instead rather than blocking indefinitely on a conversion that may never happen. State explicitly in the report which of the six were measured pre- vs post-conversion
- Document explicitly, in the Session Start / Core Skills section this issue edits, that skill weight (claude-skills-288) and mandatory-count (this issue) are two separate, additive reductions to the same "loading tax" — a reader should not conflate "we cut the list" with "we made skills lighter"
- Citation requirement scope: the "keep the citation requirement" rule below applies ONLY to the SITUATIONAL six (tdd, twelve-factor, mise, nushell, agent-loop, bees) when they stay mandatory in a given category. It does NOT apply to the Part-1 always-four (anti-fabrication, restraint, git, security) — those stay mandatory but explicitly LOSE the citation requirement per Part 1 above. The two rules target disjoint skill sets; do not apply both to the same skill
- Any of the situational six that stays mandatory (in either category) keeps the citation requirement — forced-invoke has no other verification signal without it
- Report/bees comment states the measured activation rate per skill PER CATEGORY — no unmeasured claims about model capability or task-situational necessity ship into policy
- plugin.json + marketplace.json version bump for core (and claude-code if claude-code:claude-skills-benchmark's own docs change); test/check-version-bumps.nu green

## Load skills
/core:anti-fabrication, /core:git, /core:tdd, /core:twelve-factor, /core:restraint, /core:security, /core:mise, /core:nushell, /core:agent-loop, /core:bees, claude-code:claude-skills-benchmark
close_reason: Merged as PR #259 (squash commit 859d4a52d911af3aad21af45405b66ad26523a46): dropped the citation-quote requirement for anti-fabrication/restraint/git/security (Part 1); froze but did not execute an activation-benchmark design for tdd/twelve-factor/mise/nushell/agent-loop/bees (Part 2) since claude plugin eval is early-access-gated, verified independently 3 times across the pipeline. Those six skills' mandatory status is unchanged pending claude-skills-298 (295c, blocked-external), which will execute the frozen benchmark once the tool gate lifts. Gate 3 caught a real defect even in the frozen artifact: 2 of 58 eval prompts leaked verbatim phrases from their own target skill's description, invalidating the self-check claim that had said none did. title: Author comment-reviewer agent, wire into a real spawn path
description:
## Objective
Code comments should describe a function's purpose and inputs in the minimum viable language. Add a dedicated review agent that flags comments restating code, over-explaining, or omitting purpose/inputs, and proposes terser replacements.

## Design decision (made now, not left to the implementer)
Home the agent in the core plugin — plugins/core/agents/comment-reviewer.md — so its primary wiring point is Forge's own Review row in references/forge.md (core-internal, no cross-plugin coupling). Do NOT make github:pr-review's worker hard-spawn a core-plugin agent — plugins are independently installable. Instead, document an OPTIONAL hook in github:pr-review's worker prompt: "if the core plugin is installed, optionally spawn core:comment-reviewer" — never a required dependency.

Model is fable, per operator decision. Not every environment/account has fable access, so this agent's spawn instruction must document a fallback: attempt model: fable; if that spawn errors because fable isn't available, retry the identical task with model: opus. This is a capability fallback (degrade on unavailability), not the haiku->sonnet->opus escalation-on-failure ladder — don't conflate the two in the agent's frontmatter comment or docs.

## Acceptance criteria
- New agent plugins/core/agents/comment-reviewer.md — model: fable with a documented opus fallback (see above), tools Read, Grep, Edit, skills: [core:restraint, core:anti-fabrication]
- Added to Forge's Review row in references/forge.md as the required wiring point
- Optional (documented, not hard-coded) hook added to github:pr-review's worker prompt
- /core:code-review checklist item 4 (or a new item) references the new agent/dimension
- plugin.json + marketplace.json version bump for BOTH core and github — the optional hook addition to github:pr-review's worker prompt (above) is itself a github-plugin file change, so this bump is not conditional; test/check-version-bumps.nu green

## Load skills
/core:anti-fabrication, /core:git, /core:tdd, /core:twelve-factor, /core:restraint, /core:security, /core:mise, /core:nushell, /core:agent-loop, /core:bees, core:code-review

title: Test review must verify each test's precondition took effect, not just that its assertion fails cleanly
description:
## The gap

The adversarial-TDD test-review gate (the fable reviewer that reads frozen tests BEFORE the
implementer starts) asks four questions, the first being "is every assertion satisfiable at all?"

In practice that question is answered by running the tests and confirming every failure is a
clean assertion failure rather than an error or a crash. That check is necessary and not
sufficient. It cannot distinguish:

- the behavior under test is genuinely absent (correct red — the implementer's job), from
- the test's own SETUP never produced the state the assertion describes (defective red — no
  implementation can ever satisfy it).

Both present identically: a clean `Assertion with =~ failed`, zero errors, zero raises.

## Worked example (vantageex-834, 2026-08-18)

A test at `test/vantageex/services/infra_poller_test.exs` did:

    instance = insert_instance(%{host: "always-down"})
    {:ok, _} = Repo.update(ServiceInstance.changeset(instance, %{host: "always-up"}))
    ...
    {:ok, _} = Repo.update(ServiceInstance.changeset(instance, %{host: "always-down"}))

Both `Repo.update` results are discarded, so `instance` still holds its insert-time
`host: "always-down"` in memory. `Ecto.Changeset.cast/3` records a field as changed only when
the param differs from the base struct's IN-MEMORY value, so the second call diffs
"always-down" against "always-down", produces an EMPTY changeset, and issues no UPDATE at all.
The row stayed "always-up".

The subsequent `assert log4 =~ "unreachable after 1 consecutive"` was therefore unsatisfiable by
ANY implementation — the poller was polling a healthy instance and correctly reported no failure.

The failure was invisible to every existing check:
- `Repo.update` returned `{:ok, _}`. Nothing errored. An empty changeset is a silent no-op that
  reports success.
- The test failed as a clean assertion failure, indistinguishable from a correct red.
- A fable reviewer ran the file at `--max-cases 4`, saw 8 reds, traced the assertion arithmetic
  for off-by-one errors, checked for passengers and for stub-clause shadowing, and approved.

It surfaced only when a real implementation ran against it, costing the implementer a full cycle
plus a diagnostic round (it instrumented lib code, traced live polls, and reproduced the
changeset behavior in a throwaway script before escalating).

## The check to add to the reviewer brief

For each failing assertion, confirm the PRECONDITION the test sets up actually took effect —
not merely that the assertion failed cleanly. Concretely:

- A DB write in setup: did the row actually change? An `{:ok, _}` from `Repo.update` does NOT
  prove it; an empty changeset returns `{:ok, struct}` having written nothing.
- A message send: was it received by the process under test, or swallowed?
- A config `put`: is it visible to the process that reads it? (See the `\$callers` vs `\$ancestors`
  trap — `Vantageex.Config` walks `\$callers`, but `GenServer.start_link`/`start_supervised!` set
  `\$ancestors`, so a `Config.put` in a test process is invisible inside a supervised GenServer.
  Same class of silent-no-op.)
- A stub/mock: was the clause actually reached, or did it fall through?

Rephrase the gate question from "does every assertion fail cleanly?" to "for every assertion,
can I name the observable proving the state it asserts against was actually established?"

## Two smells that are cheap to grep for

1. `{:ok, _} = Repo.update(...)` where the SAME struct variable is reused in a later
   `changeset/2` call. Ecto's in-memory diff makes the second write a no-op whenever the new
   value coincides with the struct's stale value. Rebind (`{:ok, instance} = ...`) or
   `Repo.reload/1`.
2. Any setup mutation whose result is discarded with `_` and whose effect a later assertion
   depends on.

## Acceptance criteria

- The precondition check lands in the test-review brief wherever it is codified — candidates are
  `/core:agent-loop` (the P2.5 stage description) and `/core:tdd`. Pick ONE home and
  cross-reference from the other rather than duplicating.
- The two grep-able smells above are named explicitly, since they are mechanically checkable
  where the general principle is not.
- Note the limit honestly: this raises the gate's power, it does not make it complete. Some
  setup defects will still only surface against a real implementation. The goal is to catch the
  ones a careful reviewer CAN catch, not to claim the gate is now sufficient.

## Provenance

vantageex-834, 2026-08-18. Diagnosed by the P3 implementer, which correctly STOPPED and escalated
rather than editing the frozen test; confirmed independently by the sub-team leader and again by
the team lead reading the frozen file. Fixed by a fresh test-author commit (`3d176464`) touching
one line and zero assertions.
